Their bosses' favorite new AI tool got one too. A Microsoft (MSFT) outage that began midday Thursday knocked out Outlook and other workplace apps worldwide, with Downdetector logging reports from 74 countries within about an hour. By Friday, Microsoft said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress." The damage reached Microsoft's AI. Copilot couldn't access users' email, files, or calendars, and the Microsoft connectors for OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) Claude broke too. Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its Microsoft 365 apps. Your email isn't lost. Microsoft stretched its email timeout to 48 hours, so messages sent to you keep trying to deliver instead of bouncing back. There isn't much to fix on your end. Resetting your password or reinstalling Outlook won't help, though desktop Outlook may still show mail it already downloaded. If your company pays for Microsoft 365, it may be owed money. Microsoft promises 99.9% uptime, about 43 minutes of downtime a month, with credits of 25% to 100% of the monthly fee when it falls short. Your IT department has to file the claim. Microsoft is hard to replace, which is usually good news for its shareholders. Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, whose fund owns Microsoft stock, said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that Microsoft is "the gateway to how people interact with the basic workflows of a desk worker," which makes it "a much more difficult position to dislodge." Microsoft has blamed its own changes or maintenance for Microsoft 365 disruptions in at least six months this year, from a nearly 10-hour outage in January to a spam-filter update that bounced real email earlier this month. Australia's home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said Microsoft believes it's dealing with "an update that has gone awry," much like the 2024 CrowdStrike meltdown. Microsoft reached for the oldest fix in the help desk manual, saying Thursday it was "restarting affected servers to return them to service." It didn't stick. Servers that came back went down again once traffic returned. On Friday, Microsoft traced the outage to a problem from "an earlier network capacity upgrade" that surfaced after a recent network change, and said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption." The outage comes as Microsoft trims its workforce while spending heavily on AI. It offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees in October, and those who accept leave Dec. 31. CEO Satya Nadella said last year that AI writes "maybe 20%, 30%" of Microsoft's code. Microsoft says AI wasn't the culprit. It called the outage "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents" in a post on X. In a statement to Yahoo Finance, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the company regrets "the impact these outages had on those who depend on us" and that "our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward." He didn't address questions about staffing. Chris Versace, chief investment officer at Tematica Research, put the lesson simply: "The outage and how it hobbled many businesses and other enterprises is a reminder about the need for redundancies." title: What Does Microsoft (MSFT) Global Outage Mean For Its AI Infrastructure Story? - Simply Wall St
content:
For a broader view on how critical digital plumbing is being built and secured, look at the wider group of AI infrastructure stocks through 53 AI infrastructure stocks. Microsoft is a US software giant with a US$3.9 trillion market cap that supplies cloud, productivity and AI tools that many organisations now treat as core digital infrastructure. When an outage hits services like Microsoft 365 or Copilot, it effectively tests the reliability of that entire technology stack for customers worldwide. 4 things going right for Microsoft that this headline doesn't cover. The Microsoft Narrative assumes heavy AI and cloud spending can be turned into dependable, high margin usage across services like Azure, Microsoft 365 and Copilot. A global outage across those same tools stress tests whether that spending is buying reliability as well as capacity. See how the full story points towards a $629 fair value for Microsoft. The outage cuts directly across the idea that Microsoft can keep layering AI agents and usage-based pricing onto mission critical workflows without undermining trust. When collaboration tools and Copilot go dark worldwide, it highlights the Narrative risk that huge data center capex in short lived hardware does not automatically deliver resilience, especially when rivals like Alphabet and Amazon are also selling cloud capacity. Set against that, the breadth of recent AI partnerships in healthcare, finance and R&D shows why many institutions are still standardising on Microsoft as core infrastructure. For those customers the outage is a reliability red flag, yet the deep integration of Fabric, Foundry and Agent 365 into their data and processes also makes switching costly, which supports the Narrative’s focus on sticky, contracted cloud usage if Microsoft can harden its stack. Whether this incident reads as a buying opportunity or a warning shot depends entirely on which Microsoft story you believe about AI capacity, reliability and the returns on all that infrastructure spend. All of this still leaves a bigger question hanging over Microsoft, which is where current analyst models think this business ends up a few years from now and how different that looks to what headlines suggest today. title: Microsoft vs. Salesforce: One Software Stock Remains a Top Pick, the Other Has Something to Prove, Says RBC - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) sell to many of the same corporate customers, and both are betting that AI agents, software that can carry out tasks on its own, will become a major source of revenue. Today, Microsoft got an uncomfortable reminder of how much those customers rely on it. A global outage that started Thursday afternoon knocked Outlook and parts of Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services offline for millions of users, and it dragged into Friday after the first fixes didn’t hold. Microsoft says it has found no sign of malicious activity. Microsoft shares are down around 1.5% in premarket trading on Friday. Salesforce has had a tough year of its own, with the stock down about 18% year to date. RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria covers both tech giants and published notes on each this week, ahead of Microsoft’s Ignite conference (November 17-20) and Salesforce’s fiscal third-quarter report on December 2. Starting with Microsoft, the analyst expects Ignite to show how far the company has pushed AI into every layer of its business, from data centers and in-house chips to apps and security. However, he doesn’t see the event moving the stock much in the short term. The backdrop is strong. Azure grew 48% in constant currency last quarter, up from 43% the quarter before, and management has guided for 49% to 50% this quarter. Jaluria believes demand still outruns the capacity Microsoft can bring online, which makes that guidance look cautious, though the year-ago comparison is a tough one. He wants updates on capacity and on Maia 300, the custom chip unveiled in October, which Microsoft is designing to be 40% more efficient than leading GPU setups and expects to roll out at multi-gigawatt scale in 2027. Then there’s Copilot. Daily users jumped about 50% from the prior quarter and more than fivefold year over year, while customers with over 50,000 Microsoft 365 seats grew more than 8x. Jaluria thinks investors are overlooking Microsoft’s shift toward usage-based pricing, which Cowork and GitHub Copilot already use. Charging for consumption rather than per user could lift the ceiling on what Microsoft earns as agents take on more work, and he expects Ignite to add new agent-building and management tools. “Stepping back,” Jaluria summed up, “MSFT continues to be our top pick, and we believe they are a differentiated AI beneficiary across the full stack. We see Ignite as an opportunity for management to further demonstrate the depth and breadth of AI monetization across the stack.” To this end, Jaluria rates MSFT as Outperform (i.e., Buy) with a $640 price target, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 22%. (To watch Jaluria’s track record, click here) Microsoft gets a Strong Buy consensus rating on the Street, based on 35 Buys and 4 Holds. At $632.48, the average price target implies shares will gain 21% over the coming months. (See MSFT stock forecast) Salesforce gets a cooler reception. Jaluria thinks software sentiment has yet to recover, and he lists Salesforce among the application companies without clear sight of a near-term growth pickup. That’s not because the numbers are weak. Fiscal second-quarter (July quarter) revenue rose 11% YoY, cRPO grew 14% in constant currency, and net new annual order value (AOV) posted its best growth in four years. Agentforce ARR climbed to $1.5 billion, up more than 240%. What he can’t yet see is whether that momentum turns into lasting organic acceleration. Dreamforce left him slightly more upbeat. Its centerpiece, AI Force, opens Salesforce data, workflows and governance to outside AI tools through MCPs, APIs and plugins, on the argument that Salesforce’s real value lies in the business context underneath, not the screens people click on. Jaluria isn’t sure that holds up if AI model providers move into that territory, and easier outside access could eventually make Salesforce’s own apps less essential. Partner checks also suggest pricing is still being worked out. M&A is the other sticking point. Braze (about $5.66 billion), Cresta, Listen Labs and Rune Technologies push Salesforce’s M&A spending over the past 12 months to roughly $27 billion by RBC’s estimate. Each deal makes strategic sense, Jaluria says, but together they pile on integration risk just as investors want homegrown growth. He has worried about a return to “empire-building” since the Informatica deal. The stock trades at about 12x RBC’s calendar 2027 free cash flow estimate. “Valuation remains undemanding,” says Jaluria, “but the sustained M&A cadence, early-stage AI monetization, and the need to cleanly integrate multiple concurrent acquisitions make it difficult to underwrite material upside in the near-term. In our view, Salesforce needs to demonstrate that this acquisition wave translates into durable organic reacceleration before the stock can re-rate.” To this end, he rates Salesforce as Sector Perform (i.e., Neutral) with a $250 price target. Still, should the figure be met, investors will be pocketing returns of 15% a year from now. Eight other analysts join Jaluria on the sidelines, but with an additional 30 Buys, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus view. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 29%, given the average price target stands at $280.41. title: Microsoft Service Outage Gives Software Giant Black Eye - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Nasdaq Has Best Week In Two Months, But Ends Below Key Level Microsoft (MSFT) stock wobbled Friday after a widespread outage of Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook and Teams, hobbled business and government users starting midday Thursday Eastern time. By Friday afternoon, Microsoft claimed to have had the situation mostly under control. It attributed the outage to cloud server issues. Microsoft stock ended the regular session Friday up a fraction to 523.88. In morning trades on the stock market today, Microsoft fell as much as 1.8% to 513.82, before recovering. The service outage was one of the company's most prolonged disruptions. Microsoft said it had no evidence of malicious activity. The Microsoft service outage impacted users in 74 countries and generated more than 130,000 reports on Downdetector, GlobalData reported Friday. The disruption left many users without email access. Evercore ISI analyst Kirk Materne estimated that the service outage impacted about 100 million paid seats of Microsoft 365. The company could be facing claims for service credits totaling $100 million to $400 million, he said. "This is obviously just a rough estimate, but the point is that against a $90 billion+ quarter, the impact from a monetary standpoint should be relatively benign," Materne said in a client note. "That said, it was obviously a major distraction for businesses and not a great look heading into (the company's) Ignite (conference) next week." In a post on X at 10:39 a.m. Eastern time Friday, Microsoft said the company was making "encouraging recovery progress." "We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us," Microsoft said. "We will continue to share more information as we have it, and for now we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward." In a follow-up post at 1:05 p.m. Eastern time, Microsoft apologized for the disruption. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services," the company said. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions." In a later post at 3:05 p.m. Eastern, Microsoft said its infrastructure was stabilizing, but it had work to do. "We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet," it said. title: Microsoft outage causes global chaos - Yahoo Finance Singapore
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Microsoft on Friday apologized for a global outage that disrupted public services and businesses around the world, as it reported a "broad recovery" for Outlook email and other services. The company ruled out any malicious "cyber or AI" activity as the cause of the outage, which affected several Microsoft products and disrupted health care services, delayed corporate earnings reports and left schools struggling to communicate. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," Microsoft said on X, adding full services were still being restored after the outage started on Thursday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents." The disruption knocked out Microsoft products in 74 countries and territories, affecting users across the Americas and parts of Europe, Asia and Africa, according to the outage tracker Downdetector. A top UK trade union said the disruptions had a "serious impact" on the country's health care service. National Health Service staff receiving emergency calls were "unable to refer patient details in the normal way," creating a massive backlog, said Rachel Harrison, public services head at the GMB union. As the outage dragged on for hours, airlines in India warned that customer queries may not be getting through. IndiGo and Akasa Air both said on X that their email support services had been affected and that they may not be able to receive customers' emails. Immigration New Zealand said the disruption had forced a halt in the processing of all visa applications. Japan's economy, trade and industry minister Ryosei Akazawa warned of a "significant impact" of the outage as the Microsoft products were used by a "vast number of people." In London's financial district, several people interviewed by AFP said the outage exposed their dependence on Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant. "I think one of the biggest things is Copilot not working," said Yashmit Sharma, 26, an auditor. "I think this was the main bummer. And Outlook as well, of course." Sheera, 40, a risk manager at a mid-sized bank, said businesses needed to be better prepared for unexpected technology failures. "I think we need to be a little bit more careful," said Sheera, declining to give her last name. "Anything can happen: you wake up and Outlook is not working and it's the main communication we use for our global team." The Australian Computer Society (ACS) called for a national review of sovereign IT risk, with CEO Prins Ralston saying that small businesses may not have a workaround when Outlook fails. "We need to know the systems that keep this country running won't simply fall over without notice," Ralston said, according to ACS publication Information Age. On Thursday, Microsoft attributed the disruption to "elevated load" on its infrastructure. In an updated statement on Friday, it said the "incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change." "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions." Reports of problems on Downdetector had begun to decline by 0900 GMT. Microsoft initially said it was investigating outage reports "in the Americas," but later confirmed that the issue apparently affected "Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region." Azure grew 48% in the latest quarter, and management expects growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency for the December quarter. However, Microsoft also acknowledged that customer demand continues to exceed available supply, while some third-party GPU capacity deliveries have been delayed. A sustained breakout above this region could strengthen the recovery and bring $575 into focus. On the downside, $515 is the immediate support area, followed by $490–$500. The broader demand zone sits around $375–$390, although that remains well below the current trading range. The moving averages continue to provide support beneath the current price, but the recent rejection near the supply zone suggests buyers have yet to establish control. A breakout above $560 would improve the technical outlook, while a decline below $515 could weaken the recovery. Microsoft’s long-term growth story remains supported by Azure expansion, enterprise software and AI demand. However, the latest outage has highlighted operational risks, while the company’s infrastructure spending raises questions about capital efficiency and future profitability. The next phase will depend on whether Microsoft can restore customer confidence, convert AI demand into sustainable revenue and maintain cloud growth without sacrificing margins. title: MSFT Stock Slides Pre-Market as the Microsoft 365 Outage Hitting Outlook, Teams and Copilot Runs Into Day Two - FinanceFeeds
content: MSFT stock traded at $508.51 before the bell at 10:56 GMT on Friday, down 2.77% from Thursday’s close, according to Yahoo Finance. That puts Microsoft within $3.51 of the $505 bear reference FinanceFeeds set when the shares closed at $545.18 on 9 November, with a Microsoft 365 outage that began around 1 p.m. ET Thursday still unresolved. Outlook, Teams and Copilot failed for users in 74 countries, and Microsoft says it has no indication of malicious activity. Nasdaq-100 futures were flat over the same stretch, so the pre-market drop in MSFT stock is Microsoft-specific. Downdetector logged about 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak, with one tally reaching 138,058, CIO&Leader reported. Reports reached 74 countries and territories within about an hour, according to The Next Web. Microsoft tracks the incident as EX1550543 for Exchange Online and MO1550821 for the wider suite, per SecurityWeek. Japan’s government IT infrastructure was affected, Singapore’s Government Technology Agency lost email, and the Philippine Supreme Court said its operations were affected, the Associated Press reported. EV maker Workhorse postponed its earnings call, and IndiGo and Air India rerouted customer email. Microsoft said the strain came from “a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable,” with “a core process on affected servers” overwhelmed and “causing capacity loss,” according to Outlook India. At 01:48 GMT it narrowed that to the process “responsible for establishing secure connections,” ABC7 reported. A recent network configuration change coincided with the start, and Microsoft was reversing it to test whether it contributed. Microsoft reported partial recovery at 04:36 GMT but said it had “not been sustained.” A later post said its fixes were “not taking as expected,” per AP. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, wrote that “there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” Microsoft has promised a post-incident report once service is restored. Anthropic’s status page flagged elevated errors on its Microsoft 365 connector at 17:52 UTC Thursday. By 22:23 UTC it said the fault “is caused by a Microsoft 365 service incident,” with mail, calendar and search tools failing for most requests and Claude for Outlook also affected. OpenAI reported similar trouble connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, AP said. Microsoft’s own Copilot Chat and Copilot access to work data were also hit. Microsoft said the outage affected Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with Exchange Online, per AP, and that mailbox layer is what both Copilot and the third-party connectors read from. Coverage split on how MSFT stock traded Thursday, and the tape explains why. Shares stood at $528.53 just after 1 p.m. ET, then slid to $520.87 by 3:15 p.m., a 1.45% drop, according to intraday data from Fiscal.ai. They recovered to close at $523.00, up 0.36%, on 18.6 million shares against a 10-day average of 33.1 million. Friday’s pre-market drop in MSFT stock came as Nasdaq-100 futures slipped just 0.03% at 10:57 GMT, a day after Nvidia said Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive, while Alphabet, whose Google Workspace competes with Microsoft 365, rose 0.98% pre-market. A $14.49 drop across 7.43 billion shares equals about $107.6 billion of market value. Nasdaq-100 futures were flat while MSFT stock fell 2.77% pre-market, so the $107.6 billion markdown is a Microsoft-specific outage discount. The pre-market print sits below the $520.19 year-end bear case in FinanceFeeds’ 24 October Microsoft stock prediction. title: MSFT Dips 3% as Microsoft Scrambles to Resolve Historic Outlook Outage - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft (MSFT) shares edged down 3% in extended trading following Thursday’s session, as a massive global outage across Outlook and Microsoft 365 stretched past 12 hours into Friday. Investors have treated the incident largely as a temporary operational hiccup rather than a fundamental threat to Microsoft’s cloud business. The stock was already pulled back 6% from its early-November record high ($555) amid broader tech volatility and scrutiny over AI infrastructure spending. Scope & Impact: Beginning Thursday afternoon (Nov. 12), the disruption centered on Exchange Online—the backend infrastructure powering Outlook—and spilled over into Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, OneDrive, and Copilot 365. Downdetector logged roughly 200,000 user issue reports across Microsoft services, peaking at over 130,000 for Outlook alone. The prolonged blackout forced financial trading desks and exchanges (including Euronext) to revert to phone and fax communications, while disrupting airlines, schools, healthcare networks (such as the UK’s NHS), and government agencies across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Microsoft stated there is no indication of a cyberattack. After initial remediation attempts failed to take hold, Microsoft deployed a targeted patch to a connection-routing component early Friday, reporting “positive results for server stability” as it works to restart affected infrastructure and fully restore services.

Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) enters November 13, 2026, facing renewed scrutiny over its cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence investment strategy and growing competition in enterprise productivity software. Microsoft shares closed November 12 at $523, valuing the company at approximately $3.88 tn. The stock has retreated nearly 6% from its November 4 record closing price of $555.80, reflecting broader concerns about AI valuations and the profitability of expanding computing infrastructure. According to a survey of 58 Wall Street analysts, Microsoft’s average 12-month stock price target stands at $636.12, implying potential upside of 21.6%. The median forecast is $631, while individual estimates range from $440 to $870. The consensus remains strongly positive, with 53 analysts recommending Buy or Strong Buy, five assigning Hold ratings and none recommending Sell. A separate compilation covering 51 analysts produces a lower average target of $609.54, reflecting differences in coverage and methodology. StockAnalysis.com+1 Recent investment bank forecasts suggest that confidence in Microsoft’s cloud and AI businesses remains intact. However, the emphasis has shifted from measuring demand for AI services to assessing infrastructure utilization, capital efficiency and the sustainability of earnings growth. Several major investment banks revised their Microsoft forecasts upward following the company’s October earnings report, although their valuations reflect different expectations for AI monetization. Wells Fargo raised its price target from $725 to $750 while maintaining an Overweight rating. Bernstein increased its forecast from $662 to $722 and retained an Outperform recommendation. UBS established a $700 target following the quarterly results. Citi maintained a Buy rating and a $680 target in its November 12 update, focusing on Microsoft’s opportunities in enterprise AI agents, Copilot adoption and the infrastructure needed to manage autonomous workflows. Morgan Stanley, Piper Sandler, Stifel and Jefferies have maintained forecasts around $650. RBC Capital Markets has a $640 target, while Evercore ISI expects $635. These estimates represent a relatively narrow group of bullish valuations compared with the wider range of Wall Street forecasts. More conservative projections include Barclays at $610 and Guggenheim at $595. Both remain positive on the shares but assign less upside than the most optimistic investment banks. Benzinga+2 The differences increasingly concern Microsoft’s ability to convert AI-related spending into profitable revenue. Bullish forecasts place greater weight on Azure growth, enterprise AI adoption and Microsoft’s distribution advantage. More cautious valuations leave less room for further multiple expansion until higher infrastructure spending produces stronger cash returns. Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 bn for its fiscal first quarter of 2027, ended September 30, representing 19% year-over-year growth. Operating income rose 21% to $45.9 bn, while adjusted earnings per share increased 18% to $4.89. The results exceeded Wall Street expectations for both revenue and profitability. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 bn, increasing 30%, while Azure revenue surged 48%. Management attributed the cloud performance to growing demand for AI infrastructure, higher consumption of Microsoft Foundry services and improved utilization of existing computing capacity. The company expects Azure revenue growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency during its fiscal second quarter, despite delays in the delivery of third-party GPU capacity. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligations increased 73% to $677 bn. Approximately 30% of those contracted obligations are expected to convert into revenue over the following 12 months. However, commercial bookings declined 12%, primarily because the year-earlier period included substantial Azure commitments. The difference between bookings and remaining performance obligations illustrates how large cloud contracts can create significant quarterly volatility without necessarily indicating a corresponding change in underlying demand. Microsoft+1 The accelerating cloud business provides substantial support for Microsoft’s earnings outlook. The principal uncertainty concerns profitability as an increasing share of revenue comes from computing-intensive AI workloads. Microsoft’s infrastructure investment program has become one of the central considerations in institutional valuation models. Capital expenditures reached $45.2 bn during the September quarter, with approximately three-quarters allocated to shorter-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs, alongside related memory and storage equipment. Operating cash flow increased 29% to $58 bn, but free cash flow was $18.6 bn after infrastructure investment. Management expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 bn in the December quarter. Its latest guidance places calendar 2026 spending at approximately $170 bn, following delays in third-party capacity deliveries. That updated outlook is below the $175 bn to $190 bn range referenced in some secondary forecasts. Microsoft expects capital investment to accelerate again during the second half of fiscal 2027 as delayed computing capacity becomes available and additional processors are deployed. The company also reported Microsoft Cloud gross margins of 66%, reflecting a greater revenue contribution from Azure. Management expects the figure to decline to approximately 65% in the December quarter as the business mix continues to shift toward cloud infrastructure. This creates a valuation challenge. Faster Azure revenue growth can support higher earnings estimates, but additional depreciation, equipment replacement and financing costs may limit the improvement in cash generation. Current analyst estimates imply approximately $396 bn in revenue for fiscal 2027, representing growth of about 19% from fiscal 2026. Adjusted earnings are projected at around $20.01 per share, placing Microsoft’s forward earnings multiple near 26 times its latest closing price. The valuation assumes that Microsoft can maintain substantial revenue expansion while absorbing the cost of its AI infrastructure program. A slowdown in Azure growth or weaker infrastructure profitability would make that multiple more difficult to sustain. Microsoft+2 Microsoft’s latest global service disruption has introduced another risk into the stock outlook. The outage began on November 12 and continued into Asian business hours on November 13, affecting Outlook, Microsoft Teams, Exchange Online, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services. Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the United States at the peak of the disruption, with incidents reported across 74 countries and territories. The incident affected government organizations in Australia, Japan and the United States, including the U.S. House of Representatives and Australian security agencies. Indian airlines experienced interruptions to email support services, while financial institutions in Taiwan reported operational problems, including a disrupted bond repurchase transaction. OpenAI and Anthropic also experienced problems with Microsoft 365 connectors, demonstrating how failures in Microsoft’s infrastructure can affect AI services operated by other companies. Microsoft identified overloaded server processes, unexpected server failures and traffic-routing problems as contributing factors. Some restarted servers became unresponsive again when user traffic returned. By early November 13, the company reported improvements in server stability following configuration patches and traffic optimization measures, but a complete restoration had not been confirmed. Microsoft said it had found no evidence of malicious activity and planned to release a detailed post-incident report after resolving the disruption. The incident follows a Microsoft 365 outage in January 2026 and previous Azure-related disruptions, adding to questions about the resilience of increasingly interconnected enterprise systems. CIO+2 The immediate financial effect remains difficult to quantify. No verified estimate of lost revenue, customer compensation or additional operating expenses has been disclosed. Microsoft’s subscription-based business model also limits the probability of an immediate customer exodus. Large organizations face substantial switching costs because Microsoft 365 integrates email, documents, identity management, security and collaboration software. Nevertheless, repeated disruptions could influence contract renewals, enterprise procurement decisions and the willingness of customers to concentrate additional AI workloads with a single cloud provider. For investors, the longer-term risk is not necessarily the cost of one outage but whether reliability concerns weaken Microsoft’s pricing power or slow enterprise cloud adoption. Microsoft also faces increasing competition from AI developers moving beyond conversational assistants into productivity applications. On November 10, Anthropic introduced Claude Sheets and Claude Whiteboards in beta, alongside the broader availability of its interactive dashboard product, Claude Data. Claude Sheets allows users to create spreadsheets with formulas, formatting and multiple tabs through natural-language instructions. Whiteboards supports collaborative planning, while Claude Data provides interactive analysis and visualization. Anthropic also previewed Claude Meetings, an AI assistant designed to participate in meetings and automate follow-up tasks. The expansion introduces direct competition for Microsoft Excel and parts of the wider Microsoft 365 ecosystem. Microsoft 365 commercial and consumer products generated approximately $111 bn in fiscal 2026 revenue, equivalent to roughly one-third of Microsoft’s total annual sales. Under Microsoft’s previous reporting structure, Productivity and Business Processes generated $83.9 bn in operating income, accounting for approximately 54% of total company operating profit. That segment also included LinkedIn and Dynamics, so the figure should not be interpreted as Microsoft 365 operating profit alone. The commercial significance of Anthropic’s products remains uncertain. Claude Sheets currently offers simpler spreadsheet functionality than Excel and supports exporting files into Microsoft’s established formats. Enterprise deployment is also cautious. Anthropic enabled its new applications by default for Team plans but not for Enterprise customers. Microsoft retains substantial distribution advantages. More than 430 mn people use Microsoft 365 applications, while the company reports that more than 90% of Fortune 500 businesses use Microsoft 365 Copilot. These relationships make a rapid displacement of Microsoft’s productivity suite unlikely. However, AI-native applications could eventually reduce the value customers assign to conventional software licenses or limit Microsoft’s ability to increase subscription prices. The competitive relationship is also unusual because Microsoft benefits from Anthropic’s expansion. Under an infrastructure agreement announced in November 2025, Anthropic committed to purchasing $30 bn of Azure computing capacity. Consequently, Anthropic could pressure Microsoft’s application revenue while simultaneously generating substantial demand for its cloud infrastructure. The financial outcome depends on whether Microsoft’s Azure earnings from AI developers can offset any deterioration in the pricing power or growth of its productivity software business. Claude by Anthropic+2 Microsoft is expanding beyond traditional software subscriptions through enterprise AI agents, governance tools and integrated cloud infrastructure. On November 10, Microsoft and IBM announced Imagine Enterprise, a platform designed to help organizations deploy, manage and secure AI agents in regulated industries. IBM Consulting contributes more than 6,000 prebuilt AI agents and related assets, while Microsoft supplies cloud infrastructure, AI technologies and enterprise security capabilities. The partnership targets organizations requiring extensive compliance, identity management and operational controls, including financial institutions and healthcare providers. For Microsoft, the initiative creates opportunities to generate additional Azure consumption while extending the role of Microsoft Foundry, Fabric, Copilot and Agent 365 across enterprise workflows. The investment case depends on converting experimental deployments into recurring commercial demand. Governance and security capabilities may improve Microsoft’s competitive position, particularly among organizations that cannot deploy autonomous AI systems without centralized oversight. However, the new partnership has not yet established a publicly disclosed revenue contribution sufficient to assess its effect on Microsoft’s earnings forecasts. Microsoft’s Ignite conference, scheduled for November 17 to 20, is the next major opportunity for management to address questions surrounding its AI strategy. Investment banks are looking for additional evidence of enterprise Copilot adoption, improvements in agent governance and more efficient infrastructure utilization. The conference could also provide greater visibility into how Microsoft intends to monetize autonomous AI agents across Microsoft 365, Azure and its broader enterprise platform. The most important financial indicators remain Azure capacity utilization, Microsoft 365 revenue per user, cloud gross margins and free cash flow after capital expenditures. Microsoft’s growing contractual backlog provides visibility into future sales, but investors will need to determine how quickly those commitments convert into revenue and whether infrastructure spending can produce acceptable returns. The company must also demonstrate that the latest service disruption was contained and that corrective measures can reduce the probability of similar failures. Microsoft’s next quarterly results will provide a clearer assessment of whether demand for AI computing is translating into stronger profitability, rather than simply requiring additional investment. For the stock, the distinction matters. Current valuations already incorporate sustained cloud growth and continued enterprise AI adoption. Further appreciation will depend increasingly on earnings conversion, capital efficiency and Microsoft’s ability to defend its software franchises while expanding into AI infrastructure. content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) is still struggling to restore Outlook, Teams and other workplace apps after a global outage that has lasted more than 14 hours. The disruption began on Thursday and has hit users in at least 74 countries, according to Downdetector, the outage-tracking website. On Friday morning, Microsoft said it was "seeing positive results" in improving stability and capacity, and was rolling out its fixes more widely across affected regions. Earlier, it had admitted that its repairs were not producing a sustained recovery. The company blamed "elevated load" on its infrastructure: a number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, leaving the remaining machines overloaded. It said it had found no sign of malicious activity and would publish the root cause once the problem was fixed. Reports of problems with Outlook peaked at about 140,000 on Thursday evening, according to Downdetector, which is more than 2,000 times the normal level. About 43,000 reports were still coming in at 7am UK time on Friday as Europe started work. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365, the company's office software suite, which includes Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI assistant. The disruption has spread to other technology companies, with OpenAI and Anthropic both reporting problems with their own tools. Government agencies in Japan and Australia said their email systems had been affected, including Australia's domestic intelligence agency, the BBC reported. Courts in the Philippines, Singapore and North America warned that communications would be delayed. IndiGo, India's largest airline, said its email customer support was down, while its rival Air India used the moment to advertise flights on social media. The outage revives memories of July 2024, when a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers and grounded flights around the world. title: Structural Divergence in U.S. Employment Amid AI Restructuring - 富途牛牛
content: In 2026, the U.S. labor market is characterized by low layoffs and weak hiring. Microsoft and American Express are leveraging AI to optimize their workforce, and data centers are boosting the construction sector; however, entry-level white-collar positions are under pressure, real wages are declining, and risks associated with structural transformation are becoming apparent. According to Woofun AI, the U.S. labor market in fall 2026 is experiencing a profound structural divergence: despite initial jobless claims remaining at a near-57-year low of 194,000 and the overall unemployment rate standing at just 4.2%, nonfarm payrolls increased by only 29,000 jobs in September, while both hiring and separation rates have simultaneously weakened. This anomaly of "low layoffs and weak hiring" is not merely a cyclical fluctuation, but rather characterized by$Microsoft (MSFT.US)$Offering a voluntary severance package to approximately 60,000 employees,$American Express (AXP.US)$Marking a profound transformation driven by AI-powered efficiency restructuring, the company announced cuts of approximately 5% (around 3,500 employees) to its global workforce. The calmness of macro data stands in stark contrast to the aggressive micro-level behavior of firms. With about 1.7 million people continuing to claim unemployment benefits, it indicates that large-scale forced layoffs remain rare; instead, companies prefer to adjust their structures through natural attrition, such as encouraging early retirement and accepting voluntary departures without filling the vacancies. Microsoft's voluntary buyout program covers roughly a quarter of its global workforce, which is essentially a form of voluntary exit; meanwhile, American Express explicitly emphasizes preparing for AI deployment to enhance organizational agility and decision-making efficiency. According to data compiled by Woofun AI, this model of driving AI-driven efficiency restructuring through voluntary buyouts and workforce reductions is reshaping the human‑resource cost structure of tech giants, making employment relatively secure for current staff while exposing job seekers to an exceptionally challenging market environment. The polarization of the labor market has further intensified sectoral reversals. Reemployment cycles have lengthened, with those aged 20 to 24, recent graduates, and inexperienced entry-level job seekers bearing the brunt; their unemployment rates are significantly higher than the overall level. This stems from companies' cautious hiring stance: they prioritize retaining experienced staff and leverage AI tools to assign tasks previously handled by multiple junior employees to a smaller pool of highly skilled workers, thereby shrinking the number of entry-level positions. Meanwhile, the historical pattern whereby recessions are traditionally triggered by an initial contraction in interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as construction and manufacturing has shown some partial reversal. Employment in nonresidential construction has expanded markedly, driven by data-center construction, spurring a recovery in durable consumer goods manufacturing (e.g., cooling and electrical equipment). Despite a moderate contraction in residential construction, overall employment in the construction and manufacturing sectors has continued to grow net, serving as a key factor underpinning recent economic resilience, while the service sector and white-collar jobs face distinct pressures. Productivity gains have not translated into broad-based real income growth; instead, they have exacerbated distributional imbalances. Information technology, finance, and professional services are the sectors with the highest AI adoption rates. According to Census Bureau surveys, these sectors saw a pronounced upward inflection in real output per worker from late 2022 to early 2023. Together, these high-adoption industries account for roughly 15% of the workforce. Preliminary estimates suggest that about 80% to 85% of productivity gains in AI-related sectors are currently flowing to corporate profits, with only a small share passing through to real wages. As a result, nominal wages have risen by around 3.0% year over year, while the consumer price index has increased by approximately 3.7%, leading to a modest decline in real wages. Workers, long accustomed to real wage growth of about 2% to 2.5%, are feeling greater strain from major expenses such as housing and automobiles, and the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index has remained persistently low. In this self-reinforcing cycle, firms reinvest excess profits into AI infrastructure, while small businesses—accounting for more than 40 percent of employment and GDP—face heightened uncertainty. According to an NFIB survey, in September 2026 their optimism index was slightly below its long-term average, while the uncertainty index stood well above historical norms; concerns about labor quality, inflation, volatile tariff policies, and energy price shocks have made them cautious in hiring plans. In the outlook ahead, Federal Reserve policy remains a key variable. Current leading indicators have improved across the board, except for residential construction, and corporate profits remain resilient, giving the economy some capacity to absorb further rate hikes. However, if policy continues to tighten and this translates into a marked weakening of employment in construction and manufacturing, cyclical pressures could compound and exacerbate existing structural frictions. The sustained moderate decline in residential construction employment warrants close monitoring, as it has historically foreshadowed recessions. Real wage growth is unlikely to improve significantly by 2027; deep-seated structural factors—such as the negative externalities stemming from excessive government debt and spending—continue to restrain real income growth in the private sector. The market is currently in a transitional phase: blue-collar jobs are supported by data-center construction, while entry-level white-collar positions face pressure. Policy responses should prioritize lowering barriers to retraining and improving mechanisms for creating entry-level opportunities, thereby preventing an expansion of the public sector from imposing prolonged downward pressure on private-sector real incomes. The definition of "labor-market security" is being redefined, shifting from mere unemployment status to the ability to sustainably accumulate experience and achieve real income growth amid a rapidly evolving technological landscape. title: Microsoft Global Outage Disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot 365 – And The Company Scrambles To Restore Servers - TradingView
content: Microsoft’s workplace services Outlook, Teams and Copilot were down for several hours on Thursday, causing widespread disruption of work for users across regions. In a series of updates on its status page and X handle, Microsoft said its servers were experiencing “elevated load across multiple regions,” likely contributing to the connectivity errors, and that it was trying to distribute loads across other sites and pausing deployment work. “We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” according to a post on the Microsoft 365 Status’ X handle, adding that Microsoft did a full reset of all affected servers and that the fault appeared to be with a specific component that’s responsible for processing server health. Around 7 pm ET, Microsoft said that some unresponsive servers were coming online, although they may still malfunction. “We’re seeing positive results with our efforts to restart affected infrastructure and recover server availability in an isolated manner. We’re actively monitoring the performance of these portions of infrastructure to verify stability, which we suspect will support improved availability as these actions are subsequently expanded more broadly,” the company said in its latest status update at 8 pm ET. Some users also reported an outage with Amazon’s cloud services, but AWC denied it. “AWS services have been operating normally, however, an unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports,” it said in an X post. Microsoft Outlook had over 1,000 outage reports on outage tracker Downdetector as of the last check. The reports peaked around 1:30 pm ET. Microsoft 356 and Teams also had outage reports as of the last check. Microsoft shares fell 0.2% in overnight trading late Thursday. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment flipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ as several traders complained about the outage. “Dang, looks like I’m taking off the rest of the day since Microsoft shit the bed. Our entire company is currently offline. No teams, no email, no co-pilot, nothing,” said a trader. Another wrote: “$MST This should be down several percent already. Our entire business has been frozen for hours now.” A third said, “I am starting to wonder if this Microsoft problem we are having today since lunch time is bigger than what everyone thought as a simple glitch. In other catalysts for the company, semiconductor firm Cerebras said on Thursday that it will supply chips to Microsoft and in turn will use Microsoft’s cloud services. title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services - CNBC
content:
Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began. “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. On Saturday, Microsoft said it had addressed the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. The connectivity disruption stemmed from “an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade,” Microsoft said in a Friday statement. The software giant added that the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers. Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning. In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET on Friday, Microsoft noted “encouraging recovery progress” and said that “service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure” as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online. In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were “approaching normal levels,” but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure “elevated load across multiple regions,” caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure.” Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.’s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls “may be subject to long waits” as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC’s “The Exchange” that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress. “Is there something that went on that’s nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it,” Gottheimer said. Air India said it had “temporarily rerouted” emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft “believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world’s biggest IT system outages in 2024, hitting airlines, banks and more. Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. The incident highlights a business “resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making,” James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone. “We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities.” “Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals,” he said. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were “operating normally” and an “unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports.” The company referred users to its health dashboard for “accurate data.” At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had “validated an alternative service health check method” that brought some affected servers back online. “We’re now applying this change more broadly,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses.” Got a confidential news tip? title: MSFT Stock Reverses and Heads to $500 After Microsoft 365 Services Impacted by Outlook Outage - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock retreated toward $520 after a service disruption affects Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365, adding another source of uncertainty as investors reassess rising infrastructure costs, competition from Anthropic and the profitability of cloud expansion. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have extended their retreat from record highs near $560, falling toward $520 as investors confront another setback for the technology giant. The stock had recovered sharply from the $500 area following the U.S. midterm elections, but renewed concerns about infrastructure spending, competition and operational reliability have weakened sentiment. Thursday’s decline accelerated after disruptions affected several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365. Users reported difficulties accessing email, workplace collaboration tools and other cloud-based applications, while Microsoft warned that the disruption could affect service connectivity across multiple regions. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems at 1:27 p.m. ET, alongside more than 46,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 and approximately 3,000 concerning Teams. These figures represent user-submitted reports rather than confirmed numbers of affected customers. Microsoft initially said it had resolved a Teams disruption affecting North American users, but subsequently indicated that the wider connectivity issue could affect Microsoft 365 customers internationally. Although temporary service disruptions do not necessarily indicate a structural problem, the incident highlights the dependence of businesses on Microsoft’s cloud-based productivity ecosystem. The outage comes as Microsoft faces growing scrutiny over the cost and scale of its infrastructure expansion. Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that Microsoft would finance its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. Her comments extend a community-first commitment announced in January 2026, under which the company pledged to cover electricity costs and grid upgrades associated with its projects rather than transferring those expenses to local residents. Walsh oversees Microsoft’s global data-centre operations, managing approximately 15,000 employees and a multibillion-dollar investment programme. While covering infrastructure costs could reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it also reinforces the financial burden associated with expanding Azure and computing capacity. Investors increasingly want evidence that additional infrastructure can generate sufficient revenue without weakening margins and free cash flow. Competition is another emerging concern after Anthropic introduced workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google. Its products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. The company also plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central interface for workplace activities. This represents a competitive challenge for Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue, ended September 30, 2026, increasing approximately 17% year-over-year and accounting for around 30% of total company revenue. Although this includes broader commercial and consumer cloud services, it demonstrates the importance of the productivity business to Microsoft’s financial performance. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $520 today. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, while revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. However, strong earnings have not eliminated concerns about the capital required to maintain growth. Data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require substantial upfront investment, and investors increasingly want measurable returns rather than larger spending commitments. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 custom processor, reportedly targeting 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to improve rack-scale computing capacity. Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers, but development and deployment require additional investment before those efficiency gains translate into stronger profitability. Microsoft’s latest retreat reflects several overlapping concerns: service reliability, rising infrastructure costs, Anthropic’s competitive expansion and questions about future returns. The company’s strong earnings and cloud growth remain important positives, but investors are becoming increasingly selective about the financial benefits of expanding computing capacity. With MSFT retreating from $560 toward $520, the immediate technical focus shifts to whether buyers can defend the $520 area. A sustained recovery will require renewed buying interest and stronger confidence that Microsoft’s infrastructure investments can deliver profitable growth without undermining free cash flow.

title: Morgan Stanley previews next week's Microsoft (MSFT.US) Ignite conference: The "enterprise AI flywheel" faces a critical test, with five key focal points. - 富途牛牛
content: Microsoft's Ignite conference opens next week, and Morgan Stanley treats it as a review rather than a launch event. The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US)'s Ignite conference opens next week, and Morgan Stanley views it as a validation event rather than a launch event. In a forward-looking report released on Thursday, the firm maintained an "Overweight" rating and a $650 price target. The report's focus is not on new products, but on whether a closed loop can be proven to have been established: Azure provides computing power, Fabric offers an enterprise context, Foundry orchestrates models and agents, and M365 together with Copilot integrates intelligence into employees' daily workflows. Morgan Stanley refers to these four layers as the "Enterprise AI Flywheel" and believes Ignite's value lies in demonstrating that it is translating into broader production deployments and higher full-stack consumption. The conference will be held in San Francisco from November 17 to 20. The core session is scheduled for 1 p.m. EST on November 17 (2 a.m. Beijing time on November 18), followed by a sell-side Q&A with CEO Satya Nadella at 4 p.m.; on November 18 at 3 p.m., Morgan Stanley will meet with CFO Amy Hood and Vice President of Investor Relations Jonathan Neilson. The foundation is solid, but we need to clearly explain what makes it so. The report is based on the first fiscal quarter of 2027, released on October 28. Revenue for the quarter reached $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year; Azure grew 48% (at constant currency, accelerating 6 percentage points sequentially), and M365 commercial cloud accelerated to 18% (at constant currency). Operating margin was approximately 50%. According to Morgan Stanley, this mix supports its view of revenue growth "remaining in the high teens and accelerating toward the low 20s," as well as profit growth above 20%. However, Azure's 48% growth rate warrants a closer look: both the enterprise and small-to-medium business segments are strengthening simultaneously, driven by core cloud services and AI infrastructure together—not by any single customer type. Commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $677 billion, up 73% year over year, with roughly 30% expected to convert within the next 12 months. This provides strong revenue visibility and underpins management's confidence to continue increasing capital expenditures. Morgan Stanley has identified five key observations for this conference, which essentially represent a deconstruction of its "flywheel": First, Copilot's next frontier is ARPU, not seat count. The report's three-pillar thesis is: direct seat penetration, migration to E7 plans, and usage-based billing. The significance of the third pillar is that it can expand Microsoft's revenue boundaries from "software budgets" to "budgets for knowledge work and business processes." The two figures cited in the report are: Copilot's daily active users increased by approximately 50% quarter-over-quarter, and customers actively consuming credits increased by over 75% quarter-over-quarter. Second, Foundry's value has shifted from "providing you with models" to "managing how you use the models." In the first fiscal quarter, Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, and the number of customers building multi-model agentic solutions increased fivefold year over year. Based on this, Morgan Stanley believes that greater model diversity is a boon rather than a burden for Microsoft—because the more customers switch among multiple models, the more they need a unified orchestration layer. Third, Fabric operates within an "enterprise context." As the underlying model itself becomes a commodity, governed enterprise data and context become the sources of differentiation. In the first fiscal quarter, more than 19,000 customers used both Fabric and Foundry, up from just over 17,000 last quarter. While the growth rate isn't rapid, it signals that customers are willing to bring their data onto the platform. Fourth, the widespread adoption of proxies is turning security into an entry point. As proxies begin accessing corporate data and performing actions across applications, customers must manage their identities, permissions, and behaviors. Consequently, the relevance of Entra, Defender, and Purview increases, further justifying the upgrade path from M365 to E5/E7. Agent 365, unveiled at Ignite last year, marks the starting point of this trajectory. Fifth, the Maia 300 is a variable on the cost curve. As long as demand continues to exceed supply, the deployment roadmap for in-house chips, the workloads they support, and their cost advantage relative to third-party solutions will be key to determining whether Azure's product‑level gross margin can improve. Gross margins are trending lower, but that's not the whole story. Improvements at the Azure product level partially offset the structural pressure from the rising share of Azure revenue; more importantly, the additional capacity freed up through efficiency gains was allocated to Foundry and quickly monetized—thereby supporting both revenue growth and operating leverage. According to Morgan Stanley's model, the trajectory of this curve is clear: gross margin declines from 67.9% in fiscal year 2026 to 65.9% in fiscal year 2027, 64.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 63.5% in fiscal year 2029, while operating margin remains virtually unchanged—46.8%, 46.6%, 46.7%, and 47.2%. In other words, the erosion in gross margin is offset by operating leverage—this is the key to whether this round of AI-related spending can be tolerated: the market will accept a decline in gross margin only if operating margin holds steady. The $650 base-case scenario corresponds to about 26 times FY2028 EPS of $24.41. On a reported basis, 26 times is a slight premium to large-cap software peers, and a 1.2x PEG ratio is below Microsoft's historical level and that of its peers. In the bull case, at $800, this implies roughly 29 times, or $27.41; in the bear case, at $300, it implies $22.25. The probabilities derived from implied volatility of options are: approximately 23.0% of reaching above $650, about 6.1% of reaching above $800, and roughly 6.8% of falling below $300. There is virtually no disagreement in the sell-side consensus: 97% overweight, 3% neutral, and 0% underweight. This forward-looking blind spot happens to be the one the market cares about most this week: Microsoft has stopped disclosing the number of paid Copilot seats. For the three consecutive quarters prior, paid seats (which last exceeded 30 million in disclosures) were the most direct metric for outsiders to gauge the progress of its AI implementation. However, this figure disappeared from the first fiscal quarter's earnings press release and conference call. Chief Financial Officer Hood told analysts that "no update on Copilot numbers was disclosed" this quarter, instead pointing to "momentum in revenue and usage." Nadella cited a "nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter increase" in daily active users and a "more than 75% quarter-over-quarter increase" in customers consuming credits, neither of which provided any baseline figures. This coincides with Microsoft's shift in pricing. The $99 M365 E7 suite and Agent 365 have already pushed customers toward a hybrid "seat fee + metered" model; Copilot Business, sold through the cloud solution provider channel, defaults to usage-based billing for new purchases and imposes a cap of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month—arrangements originally scheduled to take effect on December 1 were postponed to January–March 2027 following partner feedback. Morgan Stanley cites "50% increase in daily active users" as evidence of demand, but without access to the underlying seat numbers, the true significance of these percentages hinges on what their denominators actually represent. Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, told the media that many organizations are "still trying to figure out exactly what this Copilot is useful for"—whether it serves as "a fancy search tool" or as an agent integrated into workflows. This very question is precisely what Ignite must address—and Morgan Stanley assumes it already has. Two conditions that must both be true simultaneously The report's logic hinges on two conditions being met simultaneously: revenue must keep pace with rising consumption after Copilot switches to a pay-as-you-go model, and capital expenditure intensity must stop increasing. Capital spending in the first fiscal quarter was $45.2 billion (including finance leases), while the company guides for over $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter and approximately $170 billion for the full fiscal year 2027; free cash flow stood at $18.6 billion, down 27% year over year, making it the only one of the three major cloud providers still posting positive free cash flow. So at Ignite, what's truly worth listening to isn't how many agent templates were announced, but three key questions: how Copilot will be priced on a metered basis; whether Foundry can maintain its position in the orchestration layer within a multi‑model world; and whether its in‑house chips can drive down the cost per unit of compute. The first two determine the revenue ceiling, while the third sets the profit floor. In another report, Citi set a price target of $680 and assigned a "buy" rating, with reasoning similar to this report: Following a strong first fiscal quarter, Azure has reached an inflection point, and the conference will focus on infrastructure, proprietary cutting-edge models, Foundry, and the Copilot+IQ strategy. The company's results for the September quarter, the first of the fiscal year that ends next June, were released late last month and showed strong revenue growth, with the Azure cloud platform expanding at an exceptionally fast pace, according to reports from Redmond Magazine, Zacks and AI Weekly. The update keeps Microsoft firmly on the radar of investors tracking AI Stocks. The results topped Wall Street expectations on both revenue and earnings, according to Zacks, and the stock rose in after-hours trading on the day of the release, as reported by Taiwan's Inside. Shares of Microsoft trade on the Nasdaq, which places the stock in the Nasdaq Composite, and it is also a constituent of the S&P 500, the [Dow Jones Industrial Average] and the Russell 1000. Yet the quarter also brought a sharp increase in capital spending, which AI Weekly put many billions of dollars for the quarter, and free cash flow declined sharply from the prior year. Microsoft reported first-quarter revenue of many billions of dollars, according to AI Weekly's summary of the release, a strong increase from the same period a year earlier. Letsdatascience, which tracked the report, likewise described strong revenue growth and exceptionally fast Azure growth. Coverage of the results tied Azure's acceleration largely to AI workloads. Microsoft has been adding data-centre capacity at a rapid pace, and much of that capacity is being consumed by companies training and running large AI models, including OpenAI, as well as by enterprise customers deploying AI features inside their own applications. Capital expenditure, including finance leases, rose to many billions of dollars in the quarter, according to AI Weekly, a record level for the company. AI Weekly's summary also referenced a fiscal-year spending guide of many billions of dollars, underlining that the pace of building is set to remain intense through the year. The heavier spending showed up directly in free cash flow. Inside reported that free cash flow fell sharply from a year earlier to many billions of dollars, even as operating cash flow remained strong on the back of higher revenue. A consequence of the spending surge that receives close attention on Wall Street is depreciation. When Microsoft acquires servers and accelerators, the cost does not hit the reported earnings all at once; instead it is spread over the useful life of the equipment. Because chips and servers have shorter lives than buildings, a spending mix weighted toward AI hardware means depreciation charges climb quickly in the years after the equipment is installed. The initial reaction was positive. Inside reported that the shares rose in after-hours trading following the release, reflecting relief that Azure growth had accelerated and that the quarter's earnings had cleared expectations. Microsoft's management has consistently described AI demand as running ahead of the capacity the company can bring online. That framing was echoed in coverage of first-quarter report, which pointed to continued supply constraints even as new data centres opened. Beyond Azure, Microsoft's productivity franchise continued to grow, supported by commercial subscriptions and the gradual rollout of Copilot AI assistants to business customers. Pricing changes and the addition of AI features have helped lift revenue per user in recent quarters. Microsoft's next scheduled earnings report, covering the December quarter, is expected in late January. Before then, the company's annual Ignite conference, typically staged in November, is a regular venue for announcements about Copilot, Azure AI services and developer tools.
